entries.text: Prologue: The Dirge

NEON ORLEANS, 2084. Tremé, at dusk. The neon comes on over the shotgun houses one sign at a time, pink and green and gold, and under it a brass band is walking slow down Claiborne Avenue with a casket on their shoulders.

Auguste "Gus" Thibodeaux. Grand Marshal of the Lagniappe Social Aid & Pleasure Club. The man who taught you to play. A Metronome raid caught him in a rehearsal room last week with a device called the Mute, and when the Hush left, the song was gone out of him, and then so was he.
This is a [[jazz funeral]]. Dirge on the way there. You know how it goes. You're in the band.
"Where y'at, baby. Come here. You walk next to me. You hold your horn up where he can see it."
The dirge goes down Claiborne under the overpass. The whole neighborhood falls in behind. Umbrellas up. Handkerchiefs out. Nobody dancing yet. Not yet.
Then the [[MoodSync]] speaker on the corner cuts out, and a white chrome van pulls across the road, and the [[Hush|the Hush]] get out.
"Unlicensed assembly. Unlicensed syncopation detected. Cease all swing. Disperse."
The band stops. Mama Roux does not. She looks at you. Everybody looks at you.

TUTORIAL: When you RIFF, PLAY, or SOLO, a timing bar sweeps across. Tap anywhere as the marker crosses the glowing ONE zone for ×1.5 damage and +10 Groove. The pocket around it is ×1.2. Miss everything and it's CLAMS (×0.6). Build Groove to 100 and your SOLO lights up.
The patrolman goes down in the street and the band, which has not stopped watching, starts up again. Slow. The dirge. The van doors open.

TUTORIAL: VAMP halves incoming damage until your next turn and restores 15% Funk. BAG uses an item. Every enemy has one weakness (×1.5) and usually one resistance (×0.5): find them and the Blue Book remembers.

The van backs up fast and takes the corner on two wheels. The band plays the last of the dirge all the way to the cemetery gates, and they lay Gus down, and then the Grand Marshal who isn't Gus lifts the umbrella.

And the trumpet cuts loose, and the snare cracks, and the whole street turns from grief to joy in the space of one bar, the way it has for two hundred years, the way Metronome will never understand. You [[cut the body loose]]. You dance him home.
Later. The Lagniappe club. Folding chairs, a coffee urn, the trophy wall. Mama Roux sets two things on the table in front of you.
"His umbrella. And his last cassette. He made it the night before the raid. Listen."
"Don't you cry too long for me, now. Dirge on the way there, dance on the way back. That's how we do."

"Listen. Metronome's building something in the Tower. They call it the Click. A perfect beat, broadcast citywide, and when it drops, every heart in Neon Orleans keeps time with it. Forever. No swing. No lagniappe. Just the grid."

"To build it they stole the [[blues scale|six Blue Notes]]. The frequencies this city's made of. Root, flat third, fourth, flat fifth, fifth, flat seventh. Six notes, six lieutenants, one in each pocket. Take 'em back. Learn to play the whole scale. And when you can, baby, you can break the Click."

"Captain Hush took Congo Square. He's got the first one. But you can't get near him with the Hush thick on every corner like they are. Go thin them out. Win three fights on the streets, and he'll come see about you himself."
You take the umbrella. It's heavier than it looks. Everything is.

Congo Square

Congo Square. The fence is down where somebody cut it. Inside, the drum circle stones, a Hush command post where the bandstand used to be, and Captain Hush in the middle, white chrome gleaming, dampener on his belt.
"By order of Metronome, this square is now a Quiet Zone."
You step onto the stones. Somewhere behind you, in the dark, somebody starts a drum. Then another. The square remembers.
Gus brought you here your first week. "This is where it starts," he said. "Every song. Every one." You lift the horn.

Captain Hush goes down on one knee. The dampener on his belt cracks and the sound comes back into the square all at once: drums, voices, a trombone from a window on Rampart Street. Metronome's man drops something small and blue-white in the dust.
A sound like a struck glass. The Root (C) hangs in the air, blue-white, and settles into your horn. "Every song starts at the root. So does this city." (1/6 Blue Notes.)
"Baby. You did it." She's at the fence with half of Tremé behind her. "The Quarter's next. Miss Odette runs Club Feu Follet on Frenchmen. Tell her Gus sent you. She'll know what that means."
French Quarter & Frenchmen unlocked. Check Travel.

"Three rounds. Hot Rod, Big Mae, then Two-Tone. The crowd decides, and the crowd likes whoever's still standing. Ready?"
Hot Rod lowers his horn and grins. "Alright. Alright." The crowd is already looking at the door, where Big Mae is ducking in.

"Sugar Desmarais. I sang backup on MoodSync for two years and I will never forgive myself. You got a band? You got a singer." (Sugar joins your band.)

The main stage of the Bourbon Strip. The licensed clubs are dark since the broadcaster went down, but the stage is still lit, and on it, forty feet of hologram folding down into something person-sized and silver.
"Welcome to the Licensed Entertainment Strip. Tonight's performance is brought to you by Metronome. Please remain in perfect time."
Her pitch is perfect. Her time is perfect. There is not one single feeling in it. The crowd on the banquette is waiting for somebody to prove that matters.
Vox Perfecta kneels on the stage, hologram flickering. The crowd on the banquette is dead silent, and then somebody whistles, off-key, and the whole Strip laughs for the first time in a year.
"That note. The blue one. I was not built to feel that. I felt that."
Her chassis is open. Inside, under the licensing chip, a hum you recognize. The second Blue Note. And a choice.

options: Reprogram her. Let her sing for real.
Shut her down. Take the Perfect Pitch Chip.
entries.picked: Reprogram her. Let her sing for real.

entries.text: You pull the licensing chip and wire the blue note straight into her voice. She stands, tries a scale, and lands the third a hair flat, on purpose, and grins like a person. "Oh," she says. "Oh, that's what it's for." Vox Perfecta will march with the second line.
A sound like a struck glass. The ♭3 (E♭) hangs in the air, blue-white, and settles into your horn. "The flat third is where the song starts to hurt, a little, on purpose." (2/6 Blue Notes.)
"Bourbon's open. Frenchmen's loud. Now, Storyville. Madame Céleste at the Velvet Lantern has a problem named Ledger, and she's been asking for you by name."

entries.text: The Velvet Lantern
"All three. Sixty years." He doesn't cry. He puts one on the piano and it plays itself, and he puts his hands over the keys without touching them, and the room goes quiet, and then it doesn't.
"Pick one. Any sheet. It's yours. And when you march on that Tower, I'm pushing my piano down Canal Street behind you, and don't argue."

entries.text: The Velvet Lantern

"Static. Cassette deck, mostly. Metronome owns my contract, which means two Repo Drone squads follow me around to make sure I don't play anywhere that isn't theirs. Walk me from here to the Chop Shop. Two blocks. If we make it, I'm out, and I'm yours."

options: "Give me a minute to get ready."

entries.text: One block down. Static scratches a drone's wreckage and it plays its own death rattle backwards. "Second squad's on Basin."
"That's the paper." He feeds the contract into his cassette deck. It comes out the other side as a loop. "I'm out. I'm in. Where we going?" (Static joins your band.)

Ledger & Sons Counting House
Down the coal chute, two flights, through a door with no handle. The vault: steel shelves of contracts floor to ceiling, every one a life, and at a brass desk in the middle, Mr. Ledger, reading.
"Every song in this district has a lienholder, and the lienholder is me. Let's discuss your balance."
He closes the book. His Chops compound every turn he's alive. Don't give him turns.
Mr. Ledger slumps over his desk. The vault is quiet except for the hum of a thousand contracts, and under it, a note.
A sound like a struck glass. The 4th (F) hangs in the air, blue-white, and settles into your horn. "The fourth leans forward. It wants to go somewhere." (3/6 Blue Notes.)
On the desk: the contracts. All of them. Every musician, every dancer, every flower seller on Basin Street. And a ledger of what they're worth, which is a great deal of money.

You strike a match. It takes a while. The smoke goes up the coal chute and all over Basin Street, and people come out on their balconies to breathe it. Storyville is free. Madame Céleste's deluxe rooms are yours forever, and she will march with the second line.

"You could have been rich. You chose to be good. In this house that's rarer than the other thing." She hands you an airboat key. "Manchac. Grand-mère Clothilde. She knows what the pylons are doing out there."
Manchac Swamp unlocked. Check Travel.

Grand-mère Clothilde's Cabin
"Come here, mon 'tit. Traiteur don't take money. But if you got some boudin, I won't say no."

"You hear that hum? That's Pump Station 13. Metronome's been testing their Click out here where they think nobody's listening. The Chrome Wolves were listening. Their alpha, Lucien, the boy with the implant, the signal got in him and turned him into something the old folks got a name for. Rougarou."
"The pups are out on the trails, feral. Put three of them down gentle and follow the tracks to the station. And mon 'tit: the rougarou runs hot already. Heat is how you reach him."
"One more thing. I need elderberry, mamou root, and the leaf I never say the name of. Three herbs, out by the cypress. Bring them and I'll bless you proper."

Pump Station 13
Pump Station 13. The test signal is a scream now, right at the edge of hearing. The wolves part for you, implants flickering, and at the center, on the pump housing, Lucien.
Or what's left of him: chrome fur, white eyes, a jaw that's more machine than mouth. Le Rougarou Chromé. It howls in perfect 4/4.
"Heat," Grand-mère said. "The implant runs hot already. Heat is how you reach him."

The rougarou falls across the pump housing and the test signal cuts out. In the silence, the chrome fur ripples and goes still, and the white eyes go brown, and Lucien looks up at you with a human face and a machine jaw.
"Where... is my pack? What did I... I can hear it. I can still hear it. In the implant. Make it stop. Or make me stop."

options: Finish him. Take the Chrome Fang.

entries.text: You bring the horn's bell down on the implant and it shatters like cheap glass. Lucien and the Chrome Wolves will join the second line.
A sound like a struck glass. The 5th (G) hangs in the air, blue-white, and settles into your horn. "The fifth holds the roof up." (4/6 Blue Notes.)

entries.who: A haint who won't stop singing
entries.text: It sings one note, perfect, forever. "They played me back," it says between breaths. "The Archivist. Played my last note on a loop until it was the only one I had. Make it stop. Make it move."
You play the dirge. Slow. The way Gus taught you: dirge on the way there. Something in the air tears, and what's left of the pain comes out of the ground.

You play the dirge against its one note until the note bends, and breaks, and becomes two notes, then a phrase, then a song. It stops singing. It says "thank you" in a speaking voice it had forgotten, and goes.

entries.text: Vane Manor
The ballroom clears. Chandeliers, a parquet floor, the debutantes lining the walls in white. At the far end, Lady Concertmaster Isolde Vane lifts a violin that is also, somehow, a blade.
"A duel? In my ballroom? How quaint. Very well. I will show you what a note sounds like when it is exactly where it belongs."

The Blue Note is in the violin. You can hear it, flat and true, under all that perfection. When she tunes to a perfect A, only an ON THE ONE hit or a SOLO gets through. When she raises the bow for a Cadenza, VAMP.
Isolde Vane lowers the violin. Her bow arm is shaking. The debutantes along the walls have forgotten to curtsy.
"Flat. I was... flat. Father never let me be flat." She looks at the violin. "It felt... I think I liked it."
A sound like a struck glass. The ♭5 (G♭) hangs in the air, blue-white, and settles into your horn. "The blue note itself. Wrong on paper. Right in the chest." (6/6 Blue Notes.)
Six notes. The whole scale, C to B♭, humming in your horn like a hive. You can feel the shape of the blues in your hands for the first time: every note the city is, in one phrase.

"The Conductor is in the Tower. Maestro Quant. He built the Click from our stolen notes, and tomorrow night he broadcasts it, and the whole city keeps perfect time forever." She sets the violin down. "Go. Take everyone. He's only ever been afraid of a crowd."
Back to the Lagniappe club. Gus said he'd be out front. Everybody else will be waiting too.

"A duel? In my ballroom? How quaint. Very well. I will show you what a note sounds like when it is exactly where it belongs."

The Blue Note is in the violin. You can hear it, flat and true, under all that perfection. When she tunes to a perfect A, only an ON THE ONE hit or a SOLO gets through. When she raises the bow for a Cadenza, VAMP.
Isolde Vane lowers the violin. Her bow arm is shaking. The debutantes along the walls have forgotten to curtsy.
"Flat. I was... flat. Father never let me be flat." She looks at the violin. "It felt... I think I liked it."
A sound like a struck glass. The ♭5 (G♭) hangs in the air, blue-white, and settles into your horn. "The blue note itself. Wrong on paper. Right in the chest." (6/6 Blue Notes.)
Six notes. The whole scale, C to B♭, humming in your horn like a hive. You can feel the shape of the blues in your hands for the first time: every note the city is, in one phrase.

"The Conductor is in the Tower. Maestro Quant. He built the Click from our stolen notes, and tomorrow night he broadcasts it, and the whole city keeps perfect time forever." She sets the violin down. "Go. Take everyone. He's only ever been afraid of a crowd."
Back to the Lagniappe club. Gus said he'd be out front. Everybody else will be waiting too.

entries.text: The Data Mausoleum
Three Crypt Keys turn. The slab slides. Below, a server farm shaped like a chapel, racks where the pews should be, and in every rack a light that is somebody's song. One of them is Gus's.
"Every song ever played in this city is catalogued below. The dead do not improvise. Soon, neither will you."
It is a machine for grief, and it has never once felt any. You are about to fix that.

The Archivist's racks go dark in a wave, floor to ceiling, and every light in them goes out, and every light in them is a song, and the songs go up through the slab and out into the cemetery like birds.
A sound like a struck glass. The ♭7 (B♭) hangs in the air, blue-white, and settles into your horn. "The flat seventh is the door you leave by, and come back through." (5/6 Blue Notes.)
Five notes. Ti-Jacques can build your legendary.
One light stays. It drifts down out of the rack and stands in front of you, and it's wearing a hat.
"Took you long enough, baby. Now go cut me loose proper."
"Listen. They got my song, but they never got my time. You hear me? They can copy the notes. They can't copy the swing. That's yours. That's the city's. Now: I got something for you."
Gus's Grand Marshal's Regalia. The sash, the fan, the hat. It still smells like cigar. (Equipped. Grit +12, Heart +60, Mojo +2.)

"One more note. The Blue Note itself. Isolde Vane's got it in that violin of hers, up in the Garden District. Get it, and then get everybody, and then come find me. I'll be out front. I'm always out front."

"He's settled. Not resting. Settled." Mambo Rosalie rings the bell. "The Garden District's security domes don't open for people like us. You'll need an invitation to the Vane ball. Static could forge one. Céleste could call a favor. The Silver Tuxedo's valet sells them."
Garden District unlocked. Check Travel.

The Bourbon Strip

The main stage of the Bourbon Strip. The licensed clubs are dark since the broadcaster went down, but the stage is still lit, and on it, forty feet of hologram folding down into something person-sized and silver.
"Welcome to the Licensed Entertainment Strip. Tonight's performance is brought to you by Metronome. Please remain in perfect time."
Her pitch is perfect. Her time is perfect. There is not one single feeling in it. The crowd on the banquette is waiting for somebody to prove that matters.
Vox Perfecta kneels on the stage, hologram flickering. The crowd on the banquette is dead silent, and then somebody whistles, off-key, and the whole Strip laughs for the first time in a year.
"That note. The blue one. I was not built to feel that. I felt that."
Her chassis is open. Inside, under the licensing chip, a hum you recognize. The second Blue Note. And a choice.

options: Reprogram her. Let her sing for real.
Shut her down. Take the Perfect Pitch Chip.
entries.picked: Reprogram her. Let her sing for real.

entries.text: You pull the licensing chip and wire the blue note straight into her voice. She stands, tries a scale, and lands the third a hair flat, on purpose, and grins like a person. "Oh," she says. "Oh, that's what it's for." Vox Perfecta will march with the second line.
A sound like a struck glass. The ♭3 (E♭) hangs in the air, blue-white, and settles into your horn. "The flat third is where the song starts to hurt, a little, on purpose." (2/6 Blue Notes.)
"Bourbon's open. Frenchmen's loud. Now, Storyville. Madame Céleste at the Velvet Lantern has a problem named Ledger, and she's been asking for you by name."
Storyville unlocked. Check Travel.

"Three rounds. Hot Rod, Big Mae, then Two-Tone. The crowd decides, and the crowd likes whoever's still standing. Ready?"
Hot Rod lowers his horn and grins. "Alright. Alright." The crowd is already looking at the door, where Big Mae is ducking in.
Big Mae laughs so hard the glasses rattle. "Child, you can play." Two-Tone is already tuning.
Two-Tone bows. The whole room is on its feet. From the back, somebody starts singing over the applause, and the applause stops to listen.
"Sugar Desmarais. I sang backup on MoodSync for two years and I will never forgive myself. You got a band? You got a singer." (Sugar joins your band.)

Six Blue Notes on the trophy wall, humming together. Gus's umbrella against the door. And outside, on Claiborne, a crowd that has been gathering since noon.

entries.text: Your second line is 3 strong. Inside the Tower, every one of them makes you stronger (+6% to all stats), and every one of them strikes when you Play the Blues.
"Umbrella up. Everybody in. Dirge on the way there, dance on the way back." He looks at the crowd. "Except this time, baby, we skip the dirge."
The drums start. The crowd steps off. You take Claiborne to Canal, Canal to Poydras, and the Tower comes up out of the glass like a needle, and the whole city falls in behind you.

entries.text: Don't you cry too long for me, now. Dirge on the way there, dance on the way back. That's how we do.
"If Mama Roux says eat, you eat. That's not advice, that's the law."
Second Line

The pendulum stops mid-swing. The Click shatters, not loud, more like a held breath finally let go, and every screen in the city goes dark, and then comes back on showing nothing at all, and the city, for the first time in a year, hears itself.
You come down the Tower stairs with the whole second line behind you and out into the Central Business District at dawn. Poydras Street. Canal. The streetcar bell rings, late, and sweet.

Trumpet. Trombone. Sousaphone. Snare and bass drum, the Big Four cracking off the glass buildings. Sugar on top of it all. The city falls in: every stoop, every balcony, every go-cup. Umbrellas up. Handkerchiefs out.
"That's how we do." He tips his hat. He's already getting hard to see in the daylight. "Dance on the way back, baby. I'll be out front."
And the dirge turns to joy, the way it always has, and Gus Thibodeaux, Grand Marshal, lifts the umbrella one more time and walks on ahead of the band into the sun, and is gone, and the song isn't.

items.title: Vox Perfecta
items.text: Sings three nights a week at Club Feu Follet, a little flat on purpose. The crowds are enormous. The Barkers are confused.

items.title: Storyville
items.text: Free. Madame Céleste marched at the front, and the Velvet Lantern's deluxe rooms are yours forever, and the piano never stops.

items.title: Lucien
items.text: Runs the Chrome Wolves through the swamp with the implant gone, howling in swing. Grand-mère Clothilde says he fixed her steps.

items.title: The Second Line
items.text: 15 strong on the night the Click broke. Everyone in it got a hat.

entries.text: THE END. The city that care forgot never forgot how to play.
Credits

entries.text: Second Line

The pendulum stops mid-swing. The Click shatters, not loud, more like a held breath finally let go, and every screen in the city goes dark, and then comes back on showing nothing at all, and the city, for the first time in a year, hears itself.
You come down the Tower stairs with the whole second line behind you and out into the Central Business District at dawn. Poydras Street. Canal. The streetcar bell rings, late, and sweet.

Trumpet. Trombone. Sousaphone. Snare and bass drum, the Big Four cracking off the glass buildings. Sugar on top of it all. The city falls in: every stoop, every balcony, every go-cup. Umbrellas up. Handkerchiefs out.
"That's how we do." He tips his hat. He's already getting hard to see in the daylight. "Dance on the way back, baby. I'll be out front."
And the dirge turns to joy, the way it always has, and Gus Thibodeaux, Grand Marshal, lifts the umbrella one more time and walks on ahead of the band into the sun, and is gone, and the song isn't.

entries.text: New Game+
The city resets like a tape rewound. Enemies are 30% stronger. You are exactly as strong as you were. Dirge on the way there.
Prologue: The Dirge

NEON ORLEANS, 2084. Tremé, at dusk. The neon comes on over the shotgun houses one sign at a time, pink and green and gold, and under it a brass band is walking slow down Claiborne Avenue with a casket on their shoulders.

Auguste "Gus" Thibodeaux. Grand Marshal of the Lagniappe Social Aid & Pleasure Club. The man who taught you to play. A Metronome raid caught him in a rehearsal room last week with a device called the Mute, and when the Hush left, the song was gone out of him, and then so was he.
This is a [[jazz funeral]]. Dirge on the way there. You know how it goes. You're in the band.
"Where y'at, baby. Come here. You walk next to me. You hold your horn up where he can see it."
The dirge goes down Claiborne under the overpass. The whole neighborhood falls in behind. Umbrellas up. Handkerchiefs out. Nobody dancing yet. Not yet.
Then the [[MoodSync]] speaker on the corner cuts out, and a white chrome van pulls across the road, and the [[Hush|the Hush]] get out.
"Unlicensed assembly. Unlicensed syncopation detected. Cease all swing. Disperse."
The band stops. Mama Roux does not. She looks at you. Everybody looks at you.

TUTORIAL: When you RIFF, PLAY, or SOLO, a timing bar sweeps across. Tap anywhere as the marker crosses the glowing ONE zone for ×1.5 damage and +10 Groove. The pocket around it is ×1.2. Miss everything and it's CLAMS (×0.6). Build Groove to 100 and your SOLO lights up.
The patrolman goes down in the street and the band, which has not stopped watching, starts up again. Slow. The dirge. The van doors open.

TUTORIAL: VAMP halves incoming damage until your next turn and restores 15% Funk. BAG uses an item. Every enemy has one weakness (×1.5) and usually one resistance (×0.5): find them and the Blue Book remembers.

The van backs up fast and takes the corner on two wheels. The band plays the last of the dirge all the way to the cemetery gates, and they lay Gus down, and then the Grand Marshal who isn't Gus lifts the umbrella.

And the trumpet cuts loose, and the snare cracks, and the whole street turns from grief to joy in the space of one bar, the way it has for two hundred years, the way Metronome will never understand. You [[cut the body loose]]. You dance him home.
Later. The Lagniappe club. Folding chairs, a coffee urn, the trophy wall. Mama Roux sets two things on the table in front of you.
"His umbrella. And his last cassette. He made it the night before the raid. Listen."
"Don't you cry too long for me, now. Dirge on the way there, dance on the way back. That's how we do."

"Listen. Metronome's building something in the Tower. They call it the Click. A perfect beat, broadcast citywide, and when it drops, every heart in Neon Orleans keeps time with it. Forever. No swing. No lagniappe. Just the grid."

"To build it they stole the [[blues scale|six Blue Notes]]. The frequencies this city's made of. Root, flat third, fourth, flat fifth, fifth, flat seventh. Six notes, six lieutenants, one in each pocket. Take 'em back. Learn to play the whole scale. And when you can, baby, you can break the Click."

"Captain Hush took Congo Square. He's got the first one. But you can't get near him with the Hush thick on every corner like they are. Go thin them out. Win three fights on the streets, and he'll come see about you himself."
You take the umbrella. It's heavier than it looks. Everything is.
Tremé
Home turf. Shotgun houses wrapped in neon, iron balconies dripping pink light, and a brass band always practicing somewhere behind a shutter.
Credits

The city resets like a tape rewound. Enemies are 60% stronger. You are exactly as strong as you were. Dirge on the way there.
Prologue: The Dirge

NEON ORLEANS, 2084. Tremé, at dusk. The neon comes on over the shotgun houses one sign at a time, pink and green and gold, and under it a brass band is walking slow down Claiborne Avenue with a casket on their shoulders.

Auguste "Gus" Thibodeaux. Grand Marshal of the Lagniappe Social Aid & Pleasure Club. The man who taught you to play. A Metronome raid caught him in a rehearsal room last week with a device called the Mute, and when the Hush left, the song was gone out of him, and then so was he.
This is a [[jazz funeral]]. Dirge on the way there. You know how it goes. You're in the band.
"Where y'at, baby. Come here. You walk next to me. You hold your horn up where he can see it."
The dirge goes down Claiborne under the overpass. The whole neighborhood falls in behind. Umbrellas up. Handkerchiefs out. Nobody dancing yet. Not yet.
Then the [[MoodSync]] speaker on the corner cuts out, and a white chrome van pulls across the road, and the [[Hush|the Hush]] get out.
"Unlicensed assembly. Unlicensed syncopation detected. Cease all swing. Disperse."
The band stops. Mama Roux does not. She looks at you. Everybody looks at you.

TUTORIAL: When you RIFF, PLAY, or SOLO, a timing bar sweeps across. Tap anywhere as the marker crosses the glowing ONE zone for ×1.5 damage and +10 Groove. The pocket around it is ×1.2. Miss everything and it's CLAMS (×0.6). Build Groove to 100 and your SOLO lights up.
The patrolman goes down in the street and the band, which has not stopped watching, starts up again. Slow. The dirge. The van doors open.

TUTORIAL: VAMP halves incoming damage until your next turn and restores 15% Funk. BAG uses an item. Every enemy has one weakness (×1.5) and usually one resistance (×0.5): find them and the Blue Book remembers.

The van backs up fast and takes the corner on two wheels. The band plays the last of the dirge all the way to the cemetery gates, and they lay Gus down, and then the Grand Marshal who isn't Gus lifts the umbrella.

And the trumpet cuts loose, and the snare cracks, and the whole street turns from grief to joy in the space of one bar, the way it has for two hundred years, the way Metronome will never understand. You [[cut the body loose]]. You dance him home.

entries.text: Metronome Tower
The second line stops at the plaza. 15 strong. The Hush at the doors look at the crowd, and the crowd looks back, and the Hush step aside, because that is what a crowd is for.
TUTORIAL: Inside the Tower, your second line gives you +25% to all stats. Reloading mid-Tower resumes at your floor.
The Lobby
Marble, chrome, a fountain that ticks. Hush Elites in gold armor. They are not writing tickets.
The Lobby
The second line surges up the stairs behind you.
The Lobby
The Server Floors
Floors of servers humming the Click. Quantizers snap everything to the grid. And in the aisles, Session Clones: corporate copies of musicians who play your instrument.
The Server Floors
The second line surges up the stairs behind you.
The Server Floors
The Studio Floor
A recording studio the size of a city block. In the hallway, a busted vending machine with a hand-lettered sign: WORKS IF YOU HIT IT.
CLUNK. The machine lights up. BEIGNETS. CAFÉ AU LAIT. SAVE POINT (UNLICENSED). It has a slot for Doubloons and a sticker that says GUS WAS HERE.
Saved. The machine blinks approvingly.
You sit on the floor with your back to the machine. The second line sits with you. For a minute, nobody counts anything.
The Booth
The control booth. Glass on all sides. The city below, every light blinking on the beat. And at the console, baton raised, the Conductor.

"Maestro Aurelius Quant. CEO. Composer. I built the Click from six stolen notes and ten thousand captured songs, and tomorrow the city will finally be in tune. Jazz is just error, repeated until someone mistook it for culture."
He raises the baton. Behind you, the second line goes quiet, and then Gus laughs, once, loud enough to echo.
The Booth
The Conductor drops the baton. The console is still lit. Above you, through the glass ceiling, the pendulum keeps swinging, because the Click doesn't need him anymore. It never did.
The second line rallies around you. Sugar sings. Mama Roux produces a thermos. You get your breath back: Heart and Funk +50%.
The Crown
The top of the Tower. A colossal chrome metronome fills the crown, pendulum swinging. The Click. It does not speak. It ticks.
Perfect Silence comes down off the pendulum like weather. Nothing you play can touch it. Not one note. But you have six.

TUTORIAL: PLAY THE BLUES. Tap each of the six notes as it lights up. The first one's free; after that it costs 100 Groove. It shatters the Silence and every member of your second line strikes. At half Heart the Click re-shields. Build Groove and play it again.
Second Line

The pendulum stops mid-swing. The Click shatters, not loud, more like a held breath finally let go, and every screen in the city goes dark, and then comes back on showing nothing at all, and the city, for the first time in a year, hears itself.
You come down the Tower stairs with the whole second line behind you and out into the Central Business District at dawn. Poydras Street. Canal. The streetcar bell rings, late, and sweet.

Trumpet. Trombone. Sousaphone. Snare and bass drum, the Big Four cracking off the glass buildings. Sugar on top of it all. The city falls in: every stoop, every balcony, every go-cup. Umbrellas up. Handkerchiefs out.
"That's how we do." He tips his hat. He's already getting hard to see in the daylight. "Dance on the way back, baby. I'll be out front."
And the dirge turns to joy, the way it always has, and Gus Thibodeaux, Grand Marshal, lifts the umbrella one more time and walks on ahead of the band into the sun, and is gone, and the song isn't.

items.title: Vox Perfecta
items.text: The main stage on Bourbon went dark and stayed dark. Then somebody put a real band on it. The Perfect Pitch Chip hums in your pocket, remembering her set.

items.title: Storyville
items.text: Still runs on your paper, and the money was good. Madame Céleste watched the second line from the balcony. She didn't march. She remembers.

items.title: Lucien
items.text: The pack scattered. The swamp hums its own tune. The Chrome Fang in your charm slot still hums at the full moon.

items.title: The Second Line
items.text: 15 strong on the night the Click broke. Everyone in it got a hat.

entries.text: THE END. The city that care forgot never forgot how to play.
Credits

entries.text: Metronome Tower
The Server Floors
The Server Floors
The Studio Floor
A recording studio the size of a city block. In the hallway, a busted vending machine with a hand-lettered sign: WORKS IF YOU HIT IT.
CLUNK. The machine lights up. BEIGNETS. CAFÉ AU LAIT. SAVE POINT (UNLICENSED). It has a slot for Doubloons and a sticker that says GUS WAS HERE.
The Booth
The control booth. Glass on all sides. The city below, every light blinking on the beat. And at the console, baton raised, the Conductor.

"Maestro Aurelius Quant. CEO. Composer. I built the Click from six stolen notes and ten thousand captured songs, and tomorrow the city will finally be in tune. Jazz is just error, repeated until someone mistook it for culture."
He raises the baton. Behind you, the second line goes quiet, and then Gus laughs, once, loud enough to echo.
The Booth
The Conductor drops the baton. The console is still lit. Above you, through the glass ceiling, the pendulum keeps swinging, because the Click doesn't need him anymore. It never did.
The second line rallies around you. Sugar sings. Mama Roux produces a thermos. You get your breath back: Heart and Funk +50%.
The Crown
The top of the Tower. A colossal chrome metronome fills the crown, pendulum swinging. The Click. It does not speak. It ticks.
Perfect Silence comes down off the pendulum like weather. Nothing you play can touch it. Not one note. But you have six.

TUTORIAL: PLAY THE BLUES. Tap each of the six notes as it lights up. The first one's free; after that it costs 100 Groove. It shatters the Silence and every member of your second line strikes. At half Heart the Click re-shields. Build Groove and play it again.
Second Line

The pendulum stops mid-swing. The Click shatters, not loud, more like a held breath finally let go, and every screen in the city goes dark, and then comes back on showing nothing at all, and the city, for the first time in a year, hears itself.
You come down the Tower stairs with the whole second line behind you and out into the Central Business District at dawn. Poydras Street. Canal. The streetcar bell rings, late, and sweet.

Trumpet. Trombone. Sousaphone. Snare and bass drum, the Big Four cracking off the glass buildings. Sugar on top of it all. The city falls in: every stoop, every balcony, every go-cup. Umbrellas up. Handkerchiefs out.
"That's how we do." He tips his hat. He's already getting hard to see in the daylight. "Dance on the way back, baby. I'll be out front."
And the dirge turns to joy, the way it always has, and Gus Thibodeaux, Grand Marshal, lifts the umbrella one more time and walks on ahead of the band into the sun, and is gone, and the song isn't.

entries.text: Metronome Tower
The Booth
The control booth. Glass on all sides. The city below, every light blinking on the beat. And at the console, baton raised, the Conductor.

"Maestro Aurelius Quant. CEO. Composer. I built the Click from six stolen notes and ten thousand captured songs, and tomorrow the city will finally be in tune. Jazz is just error, repeated until someone mistook it for culture."
He raises the baton. Behind you, the second line goes quiet, and then Gus laughs, once, loud enough to echo.
The Booth
The Conductor drops the baton. The console is still lit. Above you, through the glass ceiling, the pendulum keeps swinging, because the Click doesn't need him anymore. It never did.
The second line rallies around you. Sugar sings. Mama Roux produces a thermos. You get your breath back: Heart and Funk +50%.
The Crown
The top of the Tower. A colossal chrome metronome fills the crown, pendulum swinging. The Click. It does not speak. It ticks.
Perfect Silence comes down off the pendulum like weather. Nothing you play can touch it. Not one note. But you have six.

The Crown
The pendulum swings. You find the one again.
Second Line

The pendulum stops mid-swing. The Click shatters, not loud, more like a held breath finally let go, and every screen in the city goes dark, and then comes back on showing nothing at all, and the city, for the first time in a year, hears itself.
You come down the Tower stairs with the whole second line behind you and out into the Central Business District at dawn. Poydras Street. Canal. The streetcar bell rings, late, and sweet.

Trumpet. Trombone. Sousaphone. Snare and bass drum, the Big Four cracking off the glass buildings. Sugar on top of it all. The city falls in: every stoop, every balcony, every go-cup. Umbrellas up. Handkerchiefs out.
"That's how we do." He tips his hat. He's already getting hard to see in the daylight. "Dance on the way back, baby. I'll be out front."
And the dirge turns to joy, the way it always has, and Gus Thibodeaux, Grand Marshal, lifts the umbrella one more time and walks on ahead of the band into the sun, and is gone, and the song isn't.

items.title: Vox Perfecta
items.text: The main stage on Bourbon went dark and stayed dark. Then somebody put a real band on it. The Perfect Pitch Chip hums in your pocket, remembering her set.

items.title: Storyville
items.text: Still runs on your paper, and the money was good. Madame Céleste watched the second line from the balcony. She didn't march. She remembers.

items.title: Lucien
items.text: The pack scattered. The swamp hums its own tune. The Chrome Fang in your charm slot still hums at the full moon.

items.title: The Second Line
items.text: 15 strong on the night the Click broke. Everyone in it got a hat.

entries.text: THE END. The city that care forgot never forgot how to play.
